summary.overview: The repository has real harness mechanisms — a blocking CI gate, pytest and ruff configuration, run scripts, and per-subtree test suites — but they are wired to the old app6 core while all recent work lands in morphing/**. The three highest-impact moves: widen the CI gate to the active subtree, fix the default startup route that points at a deleted directory, and re-point the root README so project context matches the current tree.

dimensions.label: Task Understanding
dimensions.summary: Requests and scope boundaries are recoverable in session evidence, but the only authoritative context owner (the root README) describes a legacy area and documents commands that do not resolve from the repo root.

dimensions.label: Controlled Execution
dimensions.summary: A self-cleaning run script exists for the active subtree, but the project's default startup mode addresses a directory that no longer exists, and no doctor or reset route was found.

dimensions.label: Change Validation
dimensions.summary: Deep test suites and a deliberately scoped ruff gate exist for app6, but neither the blocking CI job nor the local pytest routing reaches the code that is actually changing, and no check execution was observable in the reviewed sessions.

dimensions.label: Reliable Delivery
dimensions.summary: Changes reach a real review-and-merge boundary through pull requests with CI running before merge, which was exercised in this window. The CI result, however, carries no signal about the changed subtree, and recovery rests only on an ad-hoc git bundle.

dimensions.label: Learning Capture
dimensions.summary: A bounded review completed with 48 project memory titles reviewed clean at metadata level; the session window could not attribute requests for eight of ten episodes, so repeated-work and clean-window decisions stay inside the evidence boundary and remain unobserved.

findings.title: Morphing changes merge green while the blocking CI gate only checks app6
findings.reason: Every primary hot file in the 30-day window lives under morphing/** (App.jsx, server.py, Canvas3D.jsx, analysis.py, timeline.py), and recent commits merged through pull requests are all morphing features. The blocking CI job, however, hardcodes its steps to app6: compileall -q app6, pytest -q app6/test_module app6/api/tests, ruff check app6. A grep for morphing across ci.yml, pyproject.toml, RUN_ALL.sh and RUN_PROJECT.sh returns nothing, while morphing/backend/tests already holds five test files with a documented discover route in morphing/README.md. The cheapest existing verifier therefore never runs against the code that is actually changing, and a green merge signal carries no information about the active subtree. CI execution status itself was not observed; this is the static wiring gap.
findings.aiFixPrompt:
/better-harness fix this issue

Widen the blocking CI gate in .github/workflows/ci.yml so it exercises the active morphing subtree instead of only app6. First discover which morphing checks are collectible under the CI-pinned Python (the documented route is python3 -m unittest discover -s morphing/backend/tests from morphing/README.md); then add a step running them, and extend the ruff step to cover the morphing backend. Keep the existing app6 steps and timeouts unchanged.

## Validation

- Run the new morphing test step locally in the project venv and confirm non-zero collection with passing results
- Confirm ruff check on the widened scope reports only intended findings
- Verify the workflow YAML parses (actionlint or a draft PR) and the job still completes within its timeout

findings.title: Bare pytest silently runs only two of the project's six test roots

An agent or developer who runs the most obvious validation command gets a passing result that excludes the twelve newest-area test files, and the distorted scope already propagated into the analyzer's own suggested validation targets.
findings.aiFixPrompt:

Before editing, run python -m pytest --collect-only -q per candidate root in the project venv to discover which roots are collectible without new import configuration; for roots that fail collection, record the exact import blocker rather than silently omitting them, and add the minimum conftest or rootdir setting only if collection requires it.

findings.title: Running the project's start script with no arguments fails on a deleted ui directory

findings.title: Backend registry failures vanish behind a placeholder with no log anywhere
findings.reason: morphing/backend/server.py — the hottest backend file of the window — resolves its parameter registry through two nested imports inside _registry(), each wrapped in a bare except Exception: that finally returns {"schema": "unavailable", "groups": [], "params": []}. A targeted grep found zero logging, logger, or print calls in the file, and no configured gate would flag it (CI ruff targets app6 only, and the selected rule set omits blind-except checks). The two import targets are separate copies of params.py (724 vs 747 lines, both defining registry_json()), so a real import failure in either copy is indistinguishable from an intentionally empty registry, for the API consumer and for any later debugging pass. How the frontend renders the unavailable schema was not inspected.
findings.aiFixPrompt:
/better-harness fix this issue

Make registry failures in morphing/backend/server.py _registry() attributable without changing its fallback behavior. Add a module logger and record which import path failed and why at each except, and include a machine-readable reason (failed import vs configured empty) in the unavailable placeholder payload. Then add one test under morphing/backend/tests that forces the first import path to fail and asserts the distinguishable signal.

## Validation

- Run python3 -m unittest discover -s morphing/backend/tests and confirm the new test passes
- Confirm the endpoint response still degrades safely when both imports fail
- Check ruff on the touched file reports no new issues
